newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stresses importance of engagement.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stresses importance of engagement.

text.p: National Security Adviser Sandy Berger on Thursday cited South Asia, Central Asia and Turkey as three places where U.S. engagement is "more important than ever."

In a speech outlining the six key strategic foreign policy objectives of President Bill Clinton's second term, Berger stressed that one goal is "to neither shrink from, nor become enthralled by, the inescapable reality that America can often be the decisive force for peace in the world."

"We can't be everywhere and we shouldn't do everything. But we must be prepared to engage when important interests and values are at stake when we can make a difference," he told the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.
He cited the U.S. role in bringing peace to Bosnia with the use of military troops and in using diplomacy to pursue peace in the Middle East, Northern Ireland and Central Africa.
But he also said, "there are other places where our engagement is more important than ever," specifically naming South Asia, the Caucasus-Central Asia and Turkey.

South Asia "remains not only a flashpoint for conflict but an enormous opportunity for cooperation" while "the great resource potential and strategic location of the Caucasus and Central Asia gives us a strong stake in working with others to strengthen their stability and build up our ties to the region," he said.

Berger also said "it is profoundly in our interest to help Turkey, at a strategic and cultural crossroads, remain anchored in the West, committed to democracy and working to resolve its differences peacefully with our Greek ally."
Berger did not go into detail in his speech on administration plans for engagement in these regions.

But in answering a question later he expressed concern about U.S. dependence on foreign energy sources and stressed the "extraordinary" importance to the United States of Central Asian countries like Azerbaijan, Armenia and Georgia because of the region's massive oil deposits.
The other five U.S. strategic goals named by Berger were:
-- working for an undivided, peaceful, democratic Europe by pushing NATO enlargment among other policies
-- building a strong, stable integrated Asia-Pacific community
-- dealing with the new transnational security threats such as terrorism and drug-trafficking
-- building a new open world trading system
-- ensuring that U.S. military and diplomatic establishments are funded so the president has the tools to "harness the (post-Cold War) forces of integration" into peaceful and productive pursuits.
